title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, Risk & Exceptions
author: Ava Mitchell
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls for role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) requirements, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence generation and retention workflows, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and compliance stakeholders responsible for implementing and operating controlled systems.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-owned production systems, customer-dedicated environments, and private deployments where Redwood provides the control plane or packaging.
- Includes cloud control plane services, internal admin consoles, CI/CD pipelines, telemetry pipelines, audit logs, and evidence artifacts used for external audits (SOC2/ISO/etc.).

Goals and Principles:
- Least-privilege by default: grant only the minimum permissions required for a task.
- Strong authentication: SSO + MFA for all interactive access to privileged systems.
- Tamper-evident audit trail with 1:1 mapping between actor and action.
- Data residency and retention aligned to customer contracts and regulatory requirements.
- Secure SDLC with gated approvals and automated checks to prevent insecure changes.
- Documented incident response with security-specific playbooks and evidence capture.

1) Roles, Ownership, and RBAC Model
- Role taxonomy (global):
  1. Org Admin — Full administrative scope across org-level settings (owner_team: security for account-level policy). Not used for day-to-day service ops.
  2. Security Admin — Manage security controls (IAM policies, KMS keys, audit configuration, exceptions).
  3. Infra Engineer — Infrastructure provisioning and runtime configuration for hosting and networking.
  4. Service Owner / App Owner — Owners for individual services with right-grained permissions (deploy, config, runbooks).
  5. SRE / Oncall — Operational run-time access (read/write limited to runbooks, emergency actions via ticketed elevation).
  6. Read-Only Auditor — Access to logs, dashboards, and reports for compliance reviewers.
  7. Contracted Vendor — Time-boxed, scope-limited roles with documented access justification and approvals.

- Authentication:
  - All interactive access requires SSO (SAML/OIDC). External IdP is enforced for employees and contractors.
  - MFA required for all SSO users (TOTP or hardware keys).
  - Service-to-service authentication uses mTLS where possible, otherwise short-lived service tokens minted by the internal token service.
  - SCIM provisioning is used to sync group membership from IdP; deprovisioning must be automated and validated in the weekly access review.

- Policy enforcement and governance:
  - IAM policies are expressed as least-privilege templates and stored in the infra repo.
  - All policy changes require a PR with a security reviewer and must pass automated policy linting.
  - Temporary elevated access is granted via a Just-In-Time (JIT) workflow with ticket references and automatic expiry (default 8 hours).
  - Quarterly access reviews are owned by the Security Admins; results are tracked in the compliance tracker.

RBAC Examples (directory/service level):
- Example: service-a-deploy-role -> principal: CI system + Service Owner; permissions: read artifact store, write deployment API.
- Example: audit-reader -> principal: auditors@redwood-inference.com; permissions: read-only to audit buckets and query dashboards.

2) Audit Logging
- Events to capture (minimum):
  - Authentication events (login success/failure, MFA events, SSO assertions).
  - Authorization changes (policy updates, role grants/revokes, group membership changes).
  - Administrative actions (create/delete VM/pool, KMS policy changes, key rotations, service account creation).
  - Data access to sensitive stores (secrets read, customer data exports, database query logs for PII access).
  - Deployments and CI/CD pipeline approvals and artifacts.
  - Incident-related actions and forensics exports.

- Log integrity and pipeline:
  - All audit logs are signed at ingest where supported and forwarded to the central audit cluster (immutable storage).
  - Logs are stored in region-specific buckets consistent with data residency policies; cross-region replication requires a documented exception.
  - Tamper detection: periodic integrity checks and alerting on log gaps or ingestion failures.

- Retention and tiers:
  - Audit logs (security- and compliance-grade): 365 days online, archived to WORM (Write Once Read Many) for 7 years.
  - Operational logs (metrics, traces): 90 days hot, 365 days cold.
  - Backups (DB snapshots): retention per dataset SLA; default 90 days, with archived backups for critical systems kept up to 7 years per contractual obligations.

- Access controls: auditors get read-only access to audit logs, Security Admins can request exported slices via ticket with approval logged in the ticketing system.

3) Data Residency & Retention
- Residency model:
  - Customer data is stored in the customer-selected region for hosted accounts where required. Global metadata necessary for multi-region routing is minimized and pseudonymized.
  - Private deployments follow the customer-controlled residency specification; Redwood’s control plane will operate under agreed-to residency controls.

- Retention policy (default):
  - Customer content (models, inputs/outputs): default 90 days unless contractually extended.
  - Embeddings and derivative artifacts: 90 days default; retention extension requires explicit customer opt-in and legal review.
  - Audit logs: per audit logging section (365 days/7 years archive).
  - Personal data (employee HR records): retained in HR system per HR policy (7 years).

- Data deletion & erasure:
  - Deletion requests are executed through orchestrated pipelines that remove records from primary stores and initiate background scrub of backups.
  - Certified deletion is documented with deletion tickets and evidence artifacts (deletion manifest).
  - For immutable archives, a deletion exception process must be used with approval from Security Admin + Legal.

- Cross-border transfers:
  - Cross-border replication is disabled by default for customer-sensitive data.
  - Any required transfers must be documented, include transfer encryption, lawful basis, and be approved by Legal & Security.

4) Secure SDLC Requirements
- High-level gates:
  1. Threat modeling for new services handling customer data or secrets (owner: Service Owner + Security SME).
  2. Automated static analysis (SAST) on PRs for services in-scope.
  3. Dependency scanning and SBOM generation for production images.
  4. Secrets detection in PRs and CI; secrets in git trigger immediate rotation and incident workflow.
  5. Automated policy checks for infra-as-code (linting, drift detection) before merges.
  6. Manual security review for changes touching IAM, KMS, audit logging, data retention or cross-region replication.

- Release controls:
  - Canary and progressive rollout required for high-risk changes; rollback playbooks must be part of every deploy PR.
  - All production deploys must originate from a tagged CI artifact; ephemeral credentials for deploys are used and rotated per pipeline run.

- Developer hygiene:
  - Secrets must be managed via the central secrets manager (no secrets in code).
  - Privileged operations require 2-person review for changes to IAM or KMS policies.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures
- Incident classification and severity (triage):
  - Sev 1 (Security breach impacting multiple customers or sensitive data exfiltration): immediate IR lead escalation and all-hands response.
  - Sev 2 (Targeted compromise, limited customer impact): security IR team and SRE collaboration.
  - Sev 3 (Non-production or non-sensitive finding): tracked and remediated per normal change process.

- Security incident playbook (summary steps):
  1. Detect & Triage: Security monitoring, IDS, or external report.
  2. Contain: Isolate affected services (network ACLs, revoke tokens, rotate keys where necessary).
  3. Evidence Preservation: Snapshot relevant logs, take read-only forensic copies of affected VMs/containers, preserve timelines.
  4. Eradicate: Apply fixes, rotate compromised keys, remove malicious agents.
  5. Recover: Restore services using clean artifacts and validate integrity.
  6. Post-Incident Review: Document root cause, mitigation, timeline, and lessons learned.

- Forensics and evidence handling:
  - All actions taken during an investigation must be documented in the incident ticket with timestamps and actor identities.
  - Evidence artifacts (forensic snapshots, preserved logs) are stored in a sealed evidence bucket with restricted access and auditable access logs.
  - Chain-of-custody is recorded when handing evidence to external parties (e.g., law enforcement) and requires Legal approval.

- Communications:
  - External disclosure decisions are made by the Incident Commander in coordination with Legal and Communications.
  - Customer notifications follow the communication template in the incident communications appendix and comply with contractual SLA timing.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows
- Evidence types and owners: 
  - Access reviews (quarterly) — owner: Security Admin. Evidence: access review spreadsheets, SCIM sync logs.
  - Change control evidence — owner: Infra/Platform; Evidence: PRs, approval logs, deployed artifact hashes.
  - Audit log retention proof — owner: Logging Team; Evidence: storage manifests, replication logs, WORM policy configs.
  - Pen test and vulnerability scan reports — owner: Security; Evidence: signed reports, remediation tickets.

- Evidence generation and packaging:
  1. Evidence artifacts are tagged in the evidence repo with a standardized naming convention: evidence/<control>/<YYYY-MM-DD>/<artifact-id>.
  2. Each artifact includes a short metadata file (owner, control reference, generation date, retention policy).
  3. For external audits, a pre-packaged evidence bundle is produced by the Evidence Owner and deposited to the auditor-read bucket with time-limited access.

- Retention of evidence artifacts:
  - Evidence supporting annual certifications (e.g., SOC2) are retained for 3 years unless contractual obligations require longer.
  - Evidence for critical controls with legal/regulatory requirements are retained 7 years.

7) Risk, Exceptions, and Compensating Controls
- Exceptions process:
  1. Submit exception request via the exceptions tracker with technical justification, impacted controls, timebox, and compensating controls.
  2. Security reviews request and assigns risk owner. If customer data is impacted, Legal must review.
  3. Exceptions under 30 days may be approved by Security Admin; >30 days requires Security Leader + Legal sign-off.

- Compensating controls examples:
  - If cross-region replication is required before legal approval, require encrypted transit with per-tenant keys and enhanced monitoring (file-level audit).
  - If privileged access cannot be fully automated, require session recording, JIT expiration, and post-session attestation.

- Risk acceptance and monitoring:
  - Approved exceptions are tracked in the risk register with automatic reminders for re-evaluation 7 days prior to expiry.
  - Periodic risk reviews (monthly) by Security + Product for outstanding exceptions.

Appendix A — Configuration and Thresholds (table-like text):
- MFA: required for all interactive accounts.
- JIT session default expiry: 8 hours.
- Audit log online retention: 365 days.
- Audit log WORM archive: 7 years.
- Operational logs hot retention: 90 days.
- Evidence retention (certification): 3 years (default), 7 years for legal controls.
- Access review cadence: quarterly.

Appendix B — Ticketing & Evidence Links:
- Exceptions tracker: https://jira.redwood-inference.local/browse/SEC-EXC (internal)
- Evidence repo: s3://redwood-evidence-prod/
- Incident runbook: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process

Operational run steps (quick runbook):
1) Request temporary elevated access: open JIT ticket, include justification, approver, and expected duration.
2) On suspicious auth event: escalate to Security Pager, preserve logs (ticket), snapshot affected host.
3) To produce audit proof: open evidence request in the evidence repo and assign Logging Team owner.

Contacts and ownership:
- Primary security contact: security@redwood-inference.com (Security Admins team)
- Incident commander on-call: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks for rotation
- Evidence owner (Logging): logging-team@redwood-inference.com
